items.prompt:
(1) Why is a sawn timber plank still classed as a natural material?
A. Cutting makes a natural polymer synthetic
B. Sawing reshapes the existing natural material
C. A shaped object must be chemically synthesised
D. Natural classification depends on its original shape [1]

(2) Which statement explains a useful property and a limitation of window glass?
A. Transmits light and bends without breaking
B. Resists impact but blocks visible light
C. Bends readily but scratches very easily
D. Transmits light but fractures under impact [1]

(3) Why is concrete not the same material as cement?
A. Concrete is cement with no aggregate added
B. Concrete and cement differ only in drying time
C. Concrete includes cement binder and aggregate
D. Concrete is cement before it reacts with water [1]

(4) Why can a nylon strand be described both as a fibre and as a synthetic polymer?
A. Both terms describe only the strand’s origin
B. Fibre describes composition while polymer describes shape
C. They describe different aspects of nylon
D. Synthetic describes a material found in organisms [1]

(5) Why can concrete contain both ionic and covalent bonding?
A. Constituents have different chemical structures
B. Constituents must have identical bonding
C. Mixing changes all bonds to covalent
D. Water makes all constituents ionic [1]

(6) Which statement correctly relates cellulose and its origin?
A. It is synthetic because it has long chains
B. It is a natural polymer with covalent bonds
C. It is a natural mixture of small molecules
D. It is a natural polymer with ionic chains [1]

(7) Which building-material choice is linked to an appropriate property?
A. Glass windows: transmission of visible light
B. Copper cable coverings: high electrical conductivity
C. Glass bending brackets: resistance to scratching
D. Concrete flexible sheets: high compressive strength [1]

(8) Why does concrete harden after water is added to cement and aggregate?
A. Only evaporation of added water causes setting
B. Water dissolves aggregate into one homogeneous solid
C. Hydration of cement binds the aggregate
D. Cooling rather than hydration binds the ingredients [1]

(9) Which arrangement helps disperse a grease droplet in water?
A. Heads in grease, tails facing water
B. Heads and tails both inside grease
C. Heads and tails both outside grease
D. Tails in grease, heads facing water [1]

(10) Which statement correctly describes soap preparation from oil?
A. Acid neutralisation alone converts oil to soap
B. Mixing with cold water completes the reaction
C. Heating oil alone gives soap without an alkali
D. Alkaline hydrolysis produces soap and glycerol [1]

(11) Why can soap clean less efficiently in hard water?
A. Hard-water ions keep more soap dissolved
B. Insoluble scum consumes some of the soap
C. Hardness prevents any soap from forming lather
D. The soap neutralises all the water molecules [1]

(12) Which approximate dimensional range is used for nanomaterials here?
A. 1–100 nm
B. 1–100 mm
C. 1–100 cm
D. 1–100 m [1]
items.canonical_answer:
(1) B. Sawing reshapes the existing natural material. Mechanical shaping does not change the natural origin of the wood.
Distractor explanations: A: Cutting changes shape without synthesising new polymer chains. C: Shaping does not imply chemical synthesis. D: Natural origin is not lost when the material is reshaped.

(2) D. Transmits light but fractures under impact. Transparency suits windows; brittleness limits impact resistance.
Distractor explanations: A: Ordinary window glass is brittle rather than readily bendable. B: Window glass transmits light and is vulnerable to impact. C: Glass is not readily flexible; this combination misstates its behaviour.

(3) C. Concrete includes cement binder and aggregate. Cement is one ingredient of the concrete mixture.
Distractor explanations: A: Concrete contains aggregate as well as cement. B: Their composition differs, not merely drying time. D: Concrete is a mixture including aggregate, not an earlier stage of cement.

(4) C. They describe different aspects of nylon. Classification can use different criteria.
Distractor explanations: A: Fibre describes form; polymer describes molecular structure, not just origin. B: This reverses the roles of fibre and polymer. D: Synthetic means manufactured by chemical synthesis, not produced by organisms.

(5) A. Constituents have different chemical structures. Concrete is a mixture, so its constituents need not share one bonding type.
Distractor explanations: B: A mixture can retain constituents with different bonding types. C: Mixing does not convert all existing bonds into covalent bonds. D: Adding water does not make every constituent ionic.

(6) B. It is a natural polymer with covalent bonds. Natural origin is compatible with a covalent polymer structure.
Distractor explanations: A: Long chains establish polymer structure, not synthetic origin. C: Cellulose consists of macromolecular chains, not a mixture of small molecules. D: The bonds within cellulose chains are covalent, not ionic.

(7) A. Glass windows: transmission of visible light. Glass transmits light.
Distractor explanations: B: A cable covering must insulate; conducting copper would not do so. C: Scratch resistance does not overcome glass brittleness in a bending bracket. D: Compressive strength does not make concrete flexible in thin sheets.

(8) C. Hydration of cement binds the aggregate. Hydration produces the hardened binder.
Distractor explanations: A: Setting involves chemical hydration, not only loss of water. B: Aggregate is not dissolved into one homogeneous solid. D: Hydration reactions, rather than cooling, create the binding material.

(9) D. Tails in grease, heads facing water. The different molecular regions interact with grease and water respectively.
Distractor explanations: A: This reverses the hydrophilic heads and hydrophobic tails. B: Heads need contact with water to stabilise the dispersed droplet. C: Tails must interact with grease rather than both ends remaining in water.

(10) D. Alkaline hydrolysis produces soap and glycerol. Hydrolysis changes the fat or oil chemically.
Distractor explanations: A: Oil must undergo alkaline hydrolysis; acid neutralisation alone does not make soap. B: Cold water alone does not hydrolyse the oil to soap. C: Alkali is required for the specified soap-making reaction.

(11) B. Insoluble scum consumes some of the soap. Calcium/magnesium ions form insoluble soap salts.
Distractor explanations: A: Calcium and magnesium ions precipitate soap rather than keep it dissolved. C: Scum wastes soap, but sufficient extra soap can eventually form lather. D: Soap does not neutralise all water molecules; it reacts with hardness ions.

(12) A. 1–100 nm. The nanoscale range is approximately 1–100 nanometres in at least one dimension.
Distractor explanations: B: Millimetres are a million times larger than nanometres. C: Centimetres are ten million times larger than nanometres. D: Metres are a billion times larger than nanometres.

(a) Describe the orientation of cleaning molecules around grease. [2]

(b) Explain biodegradability and persistence. [2]

(c) Explain the supplied hard-water cleaning results. [3]

(d) Compare the extra product volumes needed in hard versus soft water. [2]

items.canonical_answer:
(a) Hydrophobic tails enter the grease and hydrophilic heads face the surrounding water, allowing dispersed droplets to be rinsed away.

(b) Microorganisms break down a biodegradable material, reducing persistence under suitable conditions.

(c) Soap S forms insoluble scum with hard-water ions, consuming some soap. Less soap remains available for cleaning, while D avoids that loss in the supplied trial.

(d) S needs 8 − 2 = 6 cm³ extra in hard water. D needs 2 − 2 = 0 cm³ extra.

(e) Mass broken down = initial − remaining: S = 5.0 − 1.0 = 4.0 g; D = 5.0 − 4.0 = 1.0 g.

(f) D achieves the cleaning endpoint with less product in hard water, but S shows more extensive microbial breakdown in this test. A defensible choice weighs those two findings; neither is unconditionally best. Seven-day results under one set of conditions do not establish behaviour in every environment, and no toxicity data are supplied.

items.prompt:
(a) State the dry and drained-wet masses displayed in the two balance panels in visuals/VIS-6117-3-readings.svg, retaining the displayed precision. [2]

(b) Draw a labelled setup for immersing a fabric sample in water, draining it for a fixed time, and measuring its mass. Include the water beaker and a balance kept clear of spilled water. [2]

(c) Plot water uptake against immersion time from this dataset: time/min = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5; uptake/g = 0, 1.8, 2.8, 3.4, 3.8, 4.0. Draw a smooth trend curve. A blank grid is supplied in visuals/VIS-6117-3-graph-blank.svg. [3]

(d) Calculate the water uptake from a dry mass of 10.0 g and a drained-wet mass of 14.0 g. [2]

(e) Explain why allowing each fabric sample a different draining time could bias the measured uptake, and how to improve the method. [3]

![Question stimulus](visuals/VIS-6117-3-readings.svg)

![Question stimulus](visuals/VIS-6117-3-graph-blank.svg)
items.canonical_answer:
(a) Dry mass 10.0 g; drained-wet mass 14.0 g.

(b) A fabric sample is fully immersed in a water beaker, lifted with tongs, drained on a rack for a measured fixed time, then weighed on a balance in a dry area. See visuals/VIS-6117-3-03.svg.

(c) Plot (0,0), (1,1.8), (2,2.8), (3,3.4), (4,3.8), (5,4.0). Label time/min horizontally and water uptake/g vertically. A smooth increasing curve approaches a plateau. See visuals/VIS-6117-3-graph-answer.svg.

(d) Water uptake = wet mass − dry mass = 14.0 − 10.0 = 4.0 g.

(e) Different draining times leave different amounts of surface water. Extra surface water raises the measured mass gain without representing absorption into the fabric. Use the same measured draining time and arrangement for each sample.

Part d: Subtract dry mass from wet mass (1).
Part d: 4.0 g (1); accept correct follow-through from an allowed reading.
Part e: Different surface-water retention (1).
Part e: Bias in the apparent mass gain (1).
Part e: Fixed measured draining time/consistent draining procedure (1).
